label: Gambling and the Bet
framing: Scripture never names the lottery, but it names the heart that wants wealth without work and money it has not earned. The bet promises that one night can undo a hard life, and that promise is the lie that empties the table.
cultural: Casting lots was common in the ancient world, used to divide land, choose duties, and even pick an apostle, but always as a way of submitting a decision to God, never as a wager against a neighbor. The soldiers gambling for the robe of Jesus at the foot of the cross are Scripture's sharpest picture of the bet, men playing for a stranger's last possession while the world's deepest loss unfolds above their heads.
historical: The early church and the Reformers alike warned against games of chance, seeing in them both the love of money and the wish to gain from another's loss. John Wesley, in the eighteenth century, told his societies to gain all they can by honest labor, drawing a hard line between earning and merely winning, and the church has long read the desire to get rich quick as a snare rather than a gift.
application: Be honest about what the bet is actually for, which is rarely money and usually escape. Set a hard wall between yourself and the trigger, the app, the account, the route past the machines. And if you have tried to stop and cannot, this is no longer a habit but an addiction, and addiction is not beaten by willpower alone but by help. In the United States you can reach free, confidential help any hour at SAMHSA, 1-800-662-4357.

verses.text: Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.
Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires.
Whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.
Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have.
And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots.

label: Overeating and the Table
framing: Food is a good gift, and the table is one of Scripture's most honored places. The struggle is not with eating but with the hunger underneath it, the reaching for the plate to fill what the plate was never able to fill.
cultural: In a world where most people lived near scarcity, a full table was a sign of God's blessing and a feast was an act of worship and welcome. Yet the same Scriptures that bless the table warn against the man whose god is his belly, and Israel in the wilderness learned that even bread from heaven could be hoarded and craved past what the body needed.
historical: The desert fathers of the fourth century named gluttony first among the deadly thoughts, not because eating was evil but because the appetite is the easiest desire to watch ruling a person. Through the centuries the church kept the practice of fasting, not to despise the body but to teach the soul that it can say no to a craving, and that hunger itself can be brought to God.
application: Look honestly at what you are feeding when you reach for food you do not need, which is often loneliness, boredom, or grief. Eat at a table, with people when you can, slowly enough to taste it, rather than alone and on the run. Let fasting, even in small measures, teach your appetite who is master. And treat your body as a gift to be kept, not a problem to be punished, and if the pattern has become a compulsion you cannot break, seek a doctor or counselor as an act of faith.

verses.text: Be not among gluttonous eaters of meat, for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty.
Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame.
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you. So glorify God in your body.
If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it.

label: Alcohol and Drinking
framing: Scripture blesses wine as a gift that gladdens the heart and warns in the same breath against the cup that masters a person. The line is not between drink and no drink but between the one who holds the cup and the one the cup has begun to hold.
cultural: Wine was woven through ordinary life in the ancient world, drunk at meals and weddings, used as medicine, and poured out in worship, and Jesus himself made it at Cana and shared it at the last supper. Yet the same Scriptures that honor wine paint drunkenness without mercy, from Noah uncovered in his tent to the long warning of the wise father, because a culture that loved its wine knew exactly what it cost when it ruled a man.
historical: Augustine, in the late fourth century, wrote of watching drink master his own mother before grace mastered her, and of his own slow learning that the cup must be ruled. The church has held the freedom of the gift and the warning of the snare together for two thousand years, and in the modern age has stood alongside the recovery movements that have walked countless people, one day at a time, out of the bottle and back into their lives.
application: Be honest about whether you still hold the cup or it now holds you, and trust the people who love you if they say what you cannot yet admit. If you have tried to stop and could not, that is not weakness but addiction, and addiction is healed in the open, with help, not in shame and alone. Reach out to a wise friend, a pastor, a doctor, and in the United States to free, confidential help any hour at SAMHSA, 1-800-662-4357.

verses.text: Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit.
Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise.
Do not look at wine when it is red. In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder.
Wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine, and bread to strengthen his heart.
All things are lawful for me, but I will not be dominated by anything.

label: Crude and Cutting Talk
framing: Scripture takes the tongue more seriously than we do, calling it a small thing that sets a whole life on fire. The question is not only what slips out when you are angry but what your everyday speech is quietly doing to the people who have to hear it.
cultural: In the biblical world a word carried weight we have nearly forgotten, a blessing or a curse spoken aloud was held to do real work, and the name of God was guarded with such care it was barely spoken. Into that world the wisdom writers built a whole library on the mouth, and James, writing to scattered churches, named the tongue a fire that no one can tame on his own.
historical: The desert fathers prized silence and watched their words the way a miser watches coins, knowing how much damage idle and cutting speech could do to a soul and a community. From the early monastic rules that limited talk to the Reformers who preached against coarse jesting and gossip, the church has long treated the mouth not as a small matter of manners but as a window straight into the heart.
application: Out of the heart the mouth speaks, so the cure runs deeper than a swear jar. Notice when the crude word, the cutting joke, the easy gossip rises, and ask what it is feeding, contempt, insecurity, the wish to be liked. Aim your speech at building the hearer up rather than scoring the point. And when you wound with words, go back and say so plainly, because the tongue that can curse can also bless.

verses.text: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up.
With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people. These things ought not to be so.
Put away anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.
Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue.

label: Lying and Honesty
framing: A lie is rarely told to harm. It is told to be safe, to be liked, to avoid the cost of the truth, and that is exactly why it is so hard to stop. Scripture treats truthfulness not as a rule but as the very ground people stand on with one another.
cultural: In a world without contracts and records as we know them, a person's word was their bond and the whole fabric of trade, family, and justice rested on it, which is why bearing false witness made the list of the ten great commands. The wisdom writers loathed the lying tongue, and Jesus traced deception all the way down, calling the devil the father of lies and naming himself, against him, the truth.
historical: Augustine, in the late fourth century, wrote two whole works arguing that the lie is never harmless, not even the lie that seems to help, because it corrupts the one who tells it. Across the centuries the church wrestled honestly with the hard cases, the hidden refugee, the murderer at the door, yet held the line that truth is the air trust breathes, and that a people who lie to each other cannot finally live together.
application: Start by telling the truth to yourself about why you lie, which is almost always fear of what the truth will cost. Practice the small honesties, the admitted mistake, the unflattering fact, since the habit of truth is built in the little things long before the large ones. Let your yes be yes. And when a lie is already told, the only way back is the hard, freeing work of going and telling the truth.

verses.text: Having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor.
Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord, but those who act faithfully are his delight.
Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices.
A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies will perish.
When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies.

label: Stealing and Taking
framing: Stealing is bigger than the empty pocket of the person robbed. It is the choice to take what you have not earned and to make another bear the cost, and Scripture answers it not only with a stop but with a strange and hopeful turn toward giving.
cultural: In an agrarian world where a stolen ox or a moved boundary stone could ruin a family, theft struck at survival itself, and the law guarded against it with care, even leaving the corners of every field unharvested so the poor could gather without stealing. Yet the prophets reserved their fiercest words not for the desperate but for the powerful who stole through crooked scales and bent courts, robbing the poor with the cover of law.
historical: The early church read the gospel as turning the thief inside out, and pointed to Zacchaeus, the tax collector who had grown rich by taking, paying back fourfold once grace reached him. Through the centuries the church taught restitution as part of real repentance, not merely feeling sorry for the theft but making it right where it could be made right, the stolen thing returned, the false gain repaid.
application: Stealing wears many coats, the padded expense, the unreported income, the small thing pocketed, the time taken on another's clock. Name yours plainly rather than dressing it up. Then do the harder thing the gospel asks, not only to stop but to repair, returning and repaying where you can. And let the deeper cure take hold, the one Paul named, working with your hands so that you have something to share, the open hand replacing the grasping one.

verses.text: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labor, so that he may have something to share.
You shall not steal.
A false balance is an abomination to the Lord, but a just weight is his delight.
If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.
You shall not oppress your neighbor or rob him.

label: Cheating and Betrayal of Trust
framing: Cheating is the quiet breaking of a promise someone trusted you to keep. Whether in a marriage, a friendship, or a sworn word, it trades a long faithfulness for a short want, and Scripture treats it as a wound to the covenant itself, not merely a private misstep.
cultural: In the biblical world the covenant was the deepest of all bonds, and marriage stood as its living picture, so much that the prophets called Israel's idolatry adultery against God himself. Into a culture that often winked at a man's wandering while punishing a woman's, Jesus traced adultery back to the look that begins it and refused to let any man stand as judge who would not first see his own heart.
historical: The church has held marriage as covenant from the start, and read faithfulness within it as a parable of God's unbreakable faithfulness to a people who keep breaking faith with him. From the early teaching on the sanctity of the vow to the Reformers who recovered marriage as a school of character, the church has named cheating clearly as betrayal, while holding out, against every instinct of the wronged heart, the possibility of repentance and the long, costly road of rebuilt trust.
application: The affair rarely begins in the bed. It begins in the small secret, the lingering conversation, the door left open that should have been shut, so guard the early ground and tell on yourself before the secret grows. If you have already broken faith, the way back is full confession, ending it completely, and patience with a trust that will be rebuilt slowly if at all. And if you are the one betrayed, you are not required to pretend, only, in time and never toward returning to harm, to begin the hardest grace of forgiving.

verses.text: You shall not commit adultery.
Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled.
He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself.
Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
So guard yourselves in your spirit, and let none of you be faithless.

label: Revenge and Getting Even
framing: The wish to get even feels like justice from the inside, but it almost never restores what was taken and almost always costs the one who carries it. Scripture does not dismiss the wrong done to you, it takes it more seriously than you do, and then asks you to hand it to a Judge who will not get it wrong.
cultural: In the honor culture of the ancient world, a wrong unanswered was a shame that clung to a whole family, and blood feuds could run for generations. The law of an eye for an eye was itself a mercy, a limit set on a revenge that always wanted more, capping repayment at the size of the wound. Into that world Jesus went further still, calling his people to turn the cheek and to love the very enemy honor demanded they destroy.
historical: The early church astonished an empire built on retaliation by refusing to return harm, blessing those who cursed them and praying for those who killed them, following a Lord who had asked forgiveness for the men driving in the nails. Across the centuries, from the martyrs to the long Christian argument over just war and mercy, the church has held that vengeance belongs to God alone, and that the wronged are freed not by getting even but by laying the debt down.
application: Name the wrong honestly rather than minimizing it, since revenge often grows where a real injury was never acknowledged. Then do the harder, freer thing, hand the case to God who judges justly, instead of appointing yourself the one who collects. This is not the same as seeking lawful justice, which can be right and good, nor does it mean returning to harm. But the score you are determined to settle will rule you long after the one who wronged you has moved on.

verses.text: Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, Vengeance is mine.
Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the Lord, and he will deliver you.
You have heard that it was said, an eye for an eye. But I say to you, do not resist the one who is evil.
Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless.
Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
